title: The Farm Laws
kicker: Three Acts on how farm produce is sold, contracted and stored
summary: Three laws let farmers sell outside government-regulated APMC mandis without state market fees, set up a framework for contract farming, and removed most stock limits on food staples. They began as ordinances in June 2020 and were passed in September. After a year of protests, Parliament repealed them in November 2021.
provisions: Trade outside APMC yards (farm gates, warehouses, cold storages and e-trading platforms) with no state market fee or cess.
Pre-sowing contracts between farmers and buyers for one season to five years, with the price stated up front. Disputes go to the SDM, with appeal to the Collector.
Cereals, pulses, oilseeds, onions and potatoes regulated only in extraordinary circumstances. Stock limits apply only after a 100% price rise (horticulture) or 50% (non-perishables).

votes.note: Passed 15 Sep (Essential Commodities) and 17 Sep (the other two). We found no recorded division count.
Passed by voice vote amid chaos. Opposition MPs say the Deputy Chairman refused their demand for a division (a recorded vote). The third bill passed on 22 Sep while most of the opposition boycotted.

committee.note: None of the three bills went to a parliamentary committee. Rajya Sabha did not adopt motions to send them to a Select Committee.

arguments_for.text: “One nation, one market”: farmers gain the freedom to sell to any buyer, anywhere, without mandi fees.
MSP and the mandi system will continue; the government offered a written assurance and said MSP procurement hit record levels.
Mandis are scarce: each one serves 496 sq km against a recommended 80 sq km, and 86% of landholdings are small or marginal. Competition could make APMCs more efficient.

arguments_against.text: Private buyers outside mandis have no duty to pay MSP. Farmers answered with “one nation, one MSP”.
Agriculture and markets are state subjects, so the Centre overrode the states.
Deregulation alone may not bring buyers: Bihar scrapped its APMC Act in 2006 and private investment did not follow.
The process was rushed: ordinances first, no committee scrutiny, and a voice vote in the Rajya Sabha.

timeline.text: Three ordinances promulgated during the COVID-19 lockdown.
Rajya Sabha passes two bills by voice vote; demand for a division refused.
“Delhi Chalo” march begins; farmers camp at Delhi’s borders for about a year.
Supreme Court stays all three laws and appoints an expert committee.
PM Modi announces repeal: “we couldn’t convince a section of farmers.”
Both Houses pass the Farm Laws Repeal Bill without debate.
Samyukt Kisan Morcha suspends the protest. It reports about 700 farmer deaths; the government says it has no record.
A new march for a legal MSP guarantee is stopped at the Punjab–Haryana border.

status.text: Repealed in November 2021. A legal guarantee for MSP, the farmers’ central demand, is still unresolved.

reflection.aye: You backed the reform. The laws passed, but they lasted 14 months: the Supreme Court suspended them and Parliament repealed them.
reflection.no: You voted against. In practice, the Rajya Sabha never counted the votes, so a “No” on 20 September was never recorded.
reflection.committee: You asked for a committee. That was the opposition’s demand on the floor, and it was refused. Even the RSS-affiliated Bharatiya Kisan Sangh wanted committee scrutiny.
reflection.abstain: You stayed out. Many opposition MPs walked out or boycotted on 22 September, and the third bill passed with almost no debate.

question: Passed without a recorded vote, repealed without a debate. How much scrutiny should a law that affects millions of farmers get?
